questions.problem:
$$
P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ 1 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrix $P$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ what are the eigenvalues and the corresponding eigenvectors of $A?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

- From the matrix $C=[\begin{aligned}-2 & -1 \\ -(-1) & -2\end{aligned}],$ we deduce that $\text{Re}(\lambda )=-2$ and $\text{Im}(\lambda )=-1.$ So, our eigenvalue is

$$
\lambda =-2+(-1)\text{i}=-2-\text{i}.
$$

- From the matrix $P=[\begin{aligned}3 & 0 \\ 5 & -2\end{aligned}],$ we deduce that our corresponding eigenvector is

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}3+0\text{i} \\ 5+(-2)\text{i}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5-2\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, the second eigenvalue of $A$ must be the complex conjugate of $\lambda ,$ and the second eigenvector must be the complex conjugate of $v.$

Therefore, our eigenvalues and eigenvectors are 

$$
\lambda =-2∓\text{i},\,v=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 5∓2\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vector $v$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $v$ is an eigenvector of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =2-3\text{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PC{P}^{-1}.$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

First, notice that 

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -3 \\ 3 & 2\end{aligned}]=C.
$$

Next, we can find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}v & =[\begin{aligned}1+2\text{i} \\ 2\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(v)}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(v)}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}2+\text{i} \\ 1-\text{i}\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the vector $v$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $v$ is an eigenvector of a $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda =3-2\text{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PC{P}^{-1}.$

$$

$$

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & -2 \\ 2 & 3\end{aligned}]\ne C,
$$

while

$$
[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) \\ -\text{Im}(\overset{―}{\lambda }) & \text{Re}(\overset{―}{\lambda })\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}3 & 2 \\ -2 & 3\end{aligned}]=C.
$$

So, our rotation-scaling matrix $C$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\overset{―}{\lambda }=3+2\text{i},$ 
 the complex conjugate of $\lambda .$ Hence, to construct the matrix $P,$ we use the eigenvector $\overset{―}{v},$ the complex conjugate of $v.$

Next, we find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{v} & =[\begin{aligned}2-\text{i} \\ 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(\overset{―}{v})}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(\overset{―}{v})}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P:$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(\overset{―}{v}) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{v}) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & -1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}

$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above.
Given that $A$ has the complex eigenvalue $\lambda =-2+2\text{i},$ and that $A=PC{P}^{-1}$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, what is the value of 
$\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

Since we are given the eigenvalue $\lambda =-2+2\text{i},$ we can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ -2 & -2\end{aligned}]
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 

$$
(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=-2+2\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-6 & -4 \\ 5 & 2\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2+2\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2+2\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}-4-2\text{i} & -4 \\ 5 & 4-2\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-4-2\text{i}){x}_{1}-4{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{1}+(4-2\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
{x}_{1}=\frac{1}{5}(-4+2\text{i}){x}_{2}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{5}(-4+2\text{i}){x}_{2} \\ {x}_{2}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{2}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{2}=5$, we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}-4+2\text{i} \\ 5\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we can construct the matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 2 \\ 5 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, 

$$
\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}=\frac{(-4)^{2}+{2}^{2}}{{5}^{2}+{0}^{2}}=\frac{4}{5}.
$$

questions.problem:
$$
A=[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 5 & 3\end{aligned}],\,P=[\begin{aligned}a & b \\ c & d\end{aligned}]
$$

Consider the matrices shown above.
Given that $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, what is the value of 
$\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}?$
questions.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2\times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PC{P}^{-1},$ where 

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}],\,C=[\begin{aligned}\text{Re}(\lambda ) & \text{Im}(\lambda ) \\ -\text{Im}(\lambda ) & \text{Re}(\lambda )\end{aligned}],
$$

and $v$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda .$

To compute the eigenvalues of $A,$ we solve the characteristic equation, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A-\lambda I) & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & -1 \\ 5 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-2\lambda +2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Using the quadratic formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda  & =\frac{-b\pm \sqrt{{b}^{2}-4ac}}{2a}=1\pm \text{i}.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's consider the eigenvalue $\lambda =1+\text{i}.$ We can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

$$
C=[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions of the matrix equation 
$(A-\lambda I)\text{x}=0.$ 
In our case, we have $\,{\lambda }_{1}=1+\text{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}-1 & -1 \\ 5 & 3\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1+\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & 1+\text{i}\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2-\text{i} & -1 \\ 5 & 2-\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(-2-\text{i}){x}_{1}-{x}_{2}=0 \\ 5{x}_{1}+(2-\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, the system above has a non-trivial solution. This implies that one row is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as free. For example, from the first equation, we get

$$
{x}_{2}=(-2-\text{i}){x}_{1}.
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

$$
[\begin{aligned}{x}_{1} \\ (-2-\text{i}){x}_{1}\end{aligned}],\,{x}_{1}\in C.
$$

Setting ${x}_{1}=1$, we get the eigenvector 

$$
v=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ -2-\text{i}\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, we can construct the matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Finally,

$$
\frac{{a}^{2}+{b}^{2}}{{c}^{2}+{d}^{2}}=\frac{{1}^{2}+{0}^{2}}{(-2)^{2}+(-1)^{2}}=\frac{1}{5}.
$$

Consider the vector $\mathbf{v}$ and the rotation-scaling matrix $C$ shown above. Given that $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of a $2 \times 2$ matrix $A$ corresponding to the eigenvalue $\lambda=2+4\textrm{i},$ find a matrix $P$ such that $A=PCP^{-1}.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2 \times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PCP^{-1},$ where 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/4a53548a17d9b4fd870ce70285bfc2c57cf6c8d352f75149e5aa7511ef4af853.png)

and $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda.$

First, notice that 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/aa5738b600440bf8327670fc21cd8005c660def232119b2b4808237d988367bd.png)

while

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/fc91fcabd47720075061e670f62be9ea9b636070a05cba70752bb7060608b764.png)

So, our rotation-scaling matrix $C$ corresponds to the eigenvalue $\overline{\lambda}=2-4\textrm{i},$ 
 the complex conjugate of $\lambda.$ Hence, to construct the matrix $P,$ we use the eigenvector $\overline{\mathbf{v}},$ the complex conjugate of $\mathbf{v}.$

Next, we find the real and imaginary parts of our eigenvector:

$$
\begin{aligned}\overset{―}{v} & =[\begin{aligned}2\text{i} \\ 7\end{aligned}]={{[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 7\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Re}(\overset{―}{v})}+\text{i}{{[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 0\end{aligned}]}_{⏟}}_{\text{Im}(\overset{―}{v})}\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can now construct $P\mathbin{:}$ 

$$
\begin{aligned}P & =[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(\overset{―}{v}) & \text{Im}(\overset{―}{v}) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 2 \\ 7 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

canonical_examples.knowledge_point: Converting a Matrix to Rotation-Scaling Form Given Only One Eigenvalue
canonical_examples.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/74cc68e763183d4599dc223cce44849ace88129bbc82b6d49bcbafc4a1a8163d.png)
Consider the matrices shown above.
Given that $A$ has the complex eigenvalue $\lambda=-2+6\textrm{i},$ and that $A=PCP^{-1}$ where $C$ is a rotation-scaling matrix, find the matrix $P.$
canonical_examples.worked_solution:
Recall that for any $2 \times 2$ real matrix $A$ with complex eigenvalues, we have $A=PCP^{-1},$ where 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/b5c1766ea1d9eb7a913fd7be2d7bf71909c81da03aaff8f4c631e1a3955f9589.png)

and $\mathbf{v}$ is an eigenvector of $A$ corresponding to the complex eigenvalue  $\lambda.$

Since we are given the eigenvalue $\lambda=-2+6\textrm{i},$ we can immediately construct the rotation-scaling matrix:

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/7f29c1c9be88268b14ef9131599420874fff6a399a3e3c92d3f4b635906163f6.png)

To compute the eigenvectors of a matrix, we need to find non-zero solutions to the matrix equation 

$$
(A - \lambda I) \textbf{x}=\mathbf{0}.
$$

 

In our case, we have $\,\lambda_1 =-2+6\textrm{i},$ and

$$
\begin{aligned}A-\lambda I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -5 \\ 9 & -5\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}-2+6\text{i} & 0 \\ 0 & -2+6\text{i}\end{aligned}] \\  & =[\begin{aligned}3-6\text{i} & -5 \\ 9 & -3-6\text{i}\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the homogeneous system of linear equations

$$
{\begin{aligned}(3-6\text{i}){x}_{1}-5{x}_{2}=0 \\ 9{x}_{1}+(-3-6\text{i}){x}_{2}=0.\end{aligned}
$$

Since the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular, the system above must have a non-zero solution. This means that one equation of the system is a multiple of another. As a result, we can drop one of the rows and take one of the variables as the free variable. For example, from the second equation, we get

$$
x_1=\dfrac 1 3(1+2\textrm{i})x_2.
$$

Hence, the general solution is given by

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/ab958a638d0bce3cb2498d6f64016e581bb303fd0df725abcfaa58dbd836b95d.png)

Setting $x_2=3$, we get the eigenvector 

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14071601/assets/631f718ed2642536c5a8e02dedc38544af5e8b6cc48bff7a0afcf77c0d057d1b.png)

Therefore, we can construct the matrix $P$ as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}P=[\begin{aligned}| & | \\ \text{Re}(v) & \text{Im}(v) \\ | & |\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 3 & 0\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$
